Antwortvariable.evidence_anchor: Increasing oak cover had generally positive effects across community dimensions and trophic groups: particularly on richness but surprisingly not on abundance.

Hauptgruppe_RoteListen.evidence_anchor: Every trophic group was significantly associated with several forest features (mean: 2.1 ±1.1sd. features) with an absolute weighted mean effect of 0.11 (±0.03) across all community dimensions and forest features (“mean effect” column in Fig. 2).

Lebensraum.evidence_anchor: The two measures of stand composition (proportion of conifers and oaks) and canopy cover had the strongest and most contrasting effects across all dimensions and trophic groups (Fig. 2).

Trend.evidence_anchor: Increasing oak cover had generally positive effects across community dimensions and trophic groups: particularly on richness but surprisingly not on abundance.

Untergruppe_RoteListen.evidence_anchor: However, for soil fungi saprotrophs and pathogens it might be due to a decrease in generalists (Appendix Fig.S5).

Antwortvariable.evidence_anchor: Most other forest features had consistent trends across the 13 groups but had fewer significant effects (all blue or all red columns in Fig. 2, Appendix Fig.S11).

Lebensraum.evidence_anchor: There were few effects on the specialisation of arthropod carnivores, omnivores and decomposers, bryophytes and symbionts because almost all species in these groups were specialist (specialisation index close to 1, Appendix Fig. S3).

Trend.evidence_anchor: High canopy cover also reduced arthropod carnivore diversity and herbivore diversity and abundance.
